records.name: Adamawa
records.current_summary: Adamawa lies within Nigeria's uniform criminalisation framework: the same-sex marriage prohibition law carries up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct and also reaches people who help arrange or attend same-sex weddings. An allied government's August 2026 travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers nationwide to Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation.  Trans-specific risk is documented nationally: mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people were reported as common, especially in northern states, and the 2024 beating-death of a prominent transgender creator in the capital evidences lethal violence against visibly trans people, with an investigation announced but no accountability recorded in the sources.  Adamawa is a far-northeastern state within the zone where the sources report some northern states operate Sharia criminal provisions that can prescribe the death penalty for same-sex conduct; the surviving evidence does not name Adamawa itself as one, and an earlier claim of documented local pressure toward such provisions could not be supported and has been removed. No state-specific incident sources survived audit, so the federal penalties and the northern climate apply without any evidenced local softening.

sources.claim: SaharaReporters (19 Aug 2026): the UK FCDO's updated travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation - same-sex conduct carries up to 14 years, some northern states apply Sharia provisions that can prescribe the death penalty, and the same-sex marriage law reaches those who help arrange or attend such weddings.

The UK government's June 2025 country-policy note on Nigeria records the framework a visitor to Adamawa stands under: same-sex sexual acts between men are criminalised with up to 14 years' imprisonment under the secular Criminal Code, and the Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act makes entering a same-sex marriage or civil union punishable by 14 years' imprisonment, with 10 years for anyone who 'administers, witnesses, abets or aides the solemnization' of one or supports the registration and operation of gay clubs and organisations. It further states that sharia penal codes apply to Muslims in the 12 northern states with death as the maximum penalty for men, that sharia courts have imposed at least four death sentences since 2022 (none carried out), and that NGOs document tens of LGBT+ arrests per year while police and Islamic police subject LGBT+ people to beatings, blackmail, extortion and torture. This is the allied-government national-framework source underpinning the record's federal-penalty and northern-climate claims for Adamawa; the note's 12-sharia-states list does not name Adamawa.

Wikipedia's Nigeria article is the national-framework source the record relies on: the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act 2013, signed into law in January 2014, makes same-sex marriage or civil union 'invalid and illegal', carries up to 14 years' imprisonment for entering one, and criminalises those who register, operate or participate in gay clubs, societies and organisations or make public show of same-sex amorous relationships; in 2022 a federal court ruled sections of the Act unconstitutional and unenforceable. The article names the 12 northern sharia-law states (Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara) where the death penalty applies to men — a list that does not include Adamawa, corroborating the record's statement that the sources do not name Adamawa as a sharia state while the federal 14-year framework and nationwide arrest climate apply.

records.name: Ekiti
records.current_summary: Ekiti lies within Nigeria's uniform criminalisation framework: the same-sex marriage prohibition law carries up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct and also reaches people who help arrange or attend same-sex weddings. An allied government's August 2026 travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers nationwide to Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation.  Trans-specific risk is evidenced nationally: a regional-magazine report on queer life in the federal capital documents threats and police raids alongside informal community organising, and community grief after the August 2024 killing of a prominent transgender creator; the report confirms that visibility itself is the trigger for enforcement and attack, a condition that travels to every state including Ekiti.  No state-specific sources for Ekiti survived audit, so no local divergence is claimed; as a southwestern state the northern Sharia provisions reported by the sources do not reach it, while the federal penalties, routine raid practice and strong church influence in local public life make concealed existence the prevailing security strategy for trans and queer residents and visitors alike.

sources.claim: SaharaReporters (19 Aug 2026): the UK FCDO's updated travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation - same-sex conduct carries up to 14 years, some northern states apply Sharia provisions that can prescribe the death penalty, and the same-sex marriage law reaches those who help arrange or attend such weddings.

Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report on the Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act documents Ekiti State enforcement on the ground: on 21 January 2014, days after the SSMPA was passed, Debbie, a 26-year-old transgender woman, was beaten by six men in Ado Ekiti, the state capital, who threatened 'You will get 14 years in prison!'; HRW reports she was beaten at least twice over the period and, unable to use Ekiti health services safely, travelled three hours each way to Ibadan for HIV treatment. The report also records a September 2014 arrest at Faguyi bar in Ado Ekiti — a gay man's third arrest, released after two days in detention by paying 2,000 Naira for himself and 10,000 Naira for a friend — and a 2014 incident in which a 25-year-old gay man was extorted by a state investigator in Ado Ekiti. These are the state-specific beatings, arrests and bribe-payments that the record's summary previously had no Ekiti source to cite.

records.name: Enugu
records.current_summary: Federal criminal law governs visitor exposure in Enugu: same-sex conduct carries up to 14 years, and the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act reaches those who arrange, attend or promote same-sex weddings or publicly promote LGBTQ+ organisations. Government travel guidance issued by a foreign ministry in August 2026 warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, and notes that mobile networks can be suspended and curfews imposed with little notice.  Reporting on queer life under those laws documents threats and police raids alongside informal community organising, and public grief after the August 2024 murder of a well-known transgender figure in the federal capital. The murder and the raids it followed were reported in the capital, not in Enugu; no Enugu-specific statute, enforcement or protection is documented in the sources examined, so the state is assessed on the nationwide framework: criminalisation on the books, arbitrary policing, and violence that is rarely prosecuted.

sources.claim: SaharaReporters (19 Aug 2026): the UK FCDO's updated travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation - same-sex conduct carries up to 14 years, some northern states apply Sharia provisions that can prescribe the death penalty, and the same-sex marriage law reaches those who help arrange or attend such weddings.

Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report documents the SSMPA's impact in Enugu State: Sharon, a bisexual woman from Enugu State, told HRW she married a male friend from high school in July 2015 under family and social pressure, saying 'For as long as I am in Nigeria, I will stay married.' An Enugu-based activist told HRW that 'the major challenge in Enugu State is the rate of HIV and STIs among members of the community' and that there are no clinics where gay men and men who have sex with men can access services without fear of harassment, forcing many to travel to Lagos and other states. This supplies the Enugu-specific social-coercion and healthcare-access findings absent from the record's existing sources.

records.name: Taraba
records.current_summary: Taraba sits under Nigeria's federal criminal law: same-sex conduct carries up to 14 years, and the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act criminalises arranging, attending or promoting same-sex weddings and registering or publicly promoting gay groups. August 2026 foreign travel guidance warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation anywhere in the country. The same reporting era records mass arrests and detentions of LGBTQ+ people as common, especially in northern states, and the August 2024 beating death of a widely followed transgender content creator in the federal capital, hours after a public post, with the murder left unsolved.  Some northern states add Sharia criminal provisions that can reach death-penalty outcomes; the audited sources do not place Taraba among the states applying them, and no Taraba-specific finding is documented either way. The visitor's profile here is the federal one: criminalisation on the statute book, arbitrary enforcement, and little protection against mob or individual violence.

sources.claim: Sahara Reporters (19 August 2026): the UK foreign office's travel advisory warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation in Nigeria - same-sex conduct carries up to 14 years federally, and some northern states' Sharia law prescribes the death penalty for it; the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act criminalises attending, organising or promoting same-sex weddings and registering or publicly promoting gay groups; the advisory also warns that mobile networks can be suspended and curfews imposed with little notice.

The English Wikipedia page 'LGBT rights in Nigeria' sets out the federal framework under which Taraba sits: same-sex sexual activity has been illegal since 1904 in the Northern Region and since 1916 region-wide, and penalty is up to 14 years' imprisonment under federal law, the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act 2014 criminalising all forms of same-sex unions as well as registering or publicly promoting gay organisations. The page lists harsher Sharia-law penalties (from lashing or caning up to death) only for states that have adopted Sharia; Taraba is not named among them, matching this record's finding that no Taraba Sharia application is documented. The page contains no Taraba-specific statute or incident; it serves as the national-framework document the state's visitor stands under.

Human Rights Watch's report of 20 October 2016, 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe: The Impact of Nigeria's Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act', records that the SSMPA, signed into law on 7 January 2014, imposes prison terms of 10 to 14 years on anyone who operates, participates in or supports gay clubs, societies or organisations, and finds that its passage was immediately followed by mob attacks, arbitrary arrests, extortion and detention of LGBT people across the country, including the arrest without charge of 21 young men at a birthday gathering in Ibadan and repeated police detentions reported by interviewees elsewhere. The report is national in scope and names no Taraba-specific case, but it substantiates the federal criminalisation and arbitrary-enforcement climate on which Taraba's visitor assessment rests.

The article records that since June 2021 Indonesia's Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue transgender Indonesians with identity papers (including the e-KTP), and it names Banten among the nine provinces whose transgender residents have benefited so far (with West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi, Lampung and Papua); the stated reasoning was that many of those people were undocumented, especially where families did not approve of their transition. For a trans visitor standing under the national framework in Banten, this documents that the province is one of the nine where identity-document issuance for transgender people has operated since mid-2021, which bears on document status and enrolment for trans travellers in this division.

records.name: Gorontalo
records.current_summary: The audited sources document Indonesia's national posture rather than Gorontalo: an October 2025 presidential decree lists "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" among non-military national-security threats alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction; legal gender change requires sex-reassignment surgery plus judicial approval; a wave of vigilante mob attacks on trans women on 14-16 July 2026 - most severely more than fifteen people doused, stripped and beaten in Bogor, with footage circulated online - and researchers record markedly hardened anti-queer attitudes since 2016. Provincial moral enforcement is sharpest in Aceh, per the same feature.  Nothing in the audited material shows Gorontalo diverging in either direction: no documented local ordinance, raid wave, protection or service specific to the province. A visitor there is exposed to the national picture - identity not criminalised, visibility treated as a security threat, mob violence met with limited accountability.

Wikipedia's country overview (LGBTQ rights in Indonesia) sets out the national framework a visitor to Gorontalo stands under: same-sex activity is not criminalised in private but carries no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protections, legal gender change requires sex-reassignment surgery plus judicial approval, and the 2022 penal-code amendment criminalising sex outside marriage - in force from 2 January 2026 - is punishable by up to one year in prison. It also independently corroborates the record's province-level claim that moral enforcement is sharpest in Aceh, noting homosexuality is illegal there under Sharia law with flogging or imprisonment, and records Indonesia voting against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025, with a 2025 Pew survey finding 93% of Indonesians rate homosexuality 'morally unacceptable'. This is the operative framework the record's 'national picture' assessment rests on, documented with dates, outcomes and a second independent source for the change-of-gender rule.
